raw_evidence.label: The time-use diary method and the 1,440-minute budget
raw_evidence.content: Time-use research rests on a simple but powerful constraint: a day has exactly 24 hours, or 1,440 minutes, and they cannot be created or destroyed — only reallocated. Unlike survey questions that ask people to estimate how much they 'usually' work or sleep (which produce notoriously inflated, socially desirable answers), the diary asks what someone was doing at each moment of a specific day. Because every activity competes for the same fixed budget, the diary captures trade-offs that stylised questions miss: more screen time must come out of something else. The MTUS harmonises diaries collected at 5-, 10-, 15-, or 30-minute intervals and on free-interval instruments into common categories, so a Korean diary from 2019 and a British diary from 1974 can be placed on the same axis.

raw_evidence.label: Why this data matters
raw_evidence.content: Time is the one resource distributed perfectly equally — everyone gets exactly 24 hours — and yet how it is spent maps almost every social inequality we care about: who does the unpaid work that keeps households running, who has leisure, who sleeps enough, how technology rewires daily life. Unpaid domestic and care work, largely invisible in GDP, has been valued at a substantial fraction of national output; the UNDP and others argue that ignoring it systematically undervalues women's contribution to the economy. Time-use diaries are the instrument that makes this invisible labour countable. A blog grounded in the MTUS is therefore a blog about fairness, measured in minutes.

sources.title: UNDP — Valuing women's unrecognized contribution to the economy
facts: Unpaid care and domestic work is largely excluded from GDP and disproportionately performed by women

raw_evidence.label: The established gender gap in unpaid work
raw_evidence.content: The single most robust finding in the time-use literature is that women perform far more unpaid domestic and care work than men, while men do more paid work — a division that persists even where women's paid employment has risen sharply. OECD analysis across countries finds women average about four hours a day of unpaid household and care work, roughly twice men's, and across 23 European countries women spend about 262 minutes versus men's 141 — a gap of roughly two hours every day. The gap varies enormously by place: under an hour a day in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, but over 200 minutes in countries such as Türkiye, Portugal and Mexico. Routine housework is the single largest component of unpaid work for both sexes. This is the benchmark against which the MTUS housework and childcare numbers should be read.

sources.title: OECD — Persistent gender gaps in paid and unpaid work
facts: Women average ~4 hours/day of unpaid work, about twice men's
Across 23 European countries women spend ~262 min vs men's 141 min on unpaid work
Gender unpaid-work gaps exceed 200 min/day in Türkiye, Portugal, Mexico and are under 60 min/day in Denmark, Norway, Sweden

raw_evidence.editorial_notes: 2.26x and the 32.5-min total-work gap must be exact. 'Second shift' framing load-bearing.

raw_evidence.label: The unpaid-work gender gap: women do 2.3x men's
raw_evidence.content: Across all 1.4 million weighted diary days, the division of labour is stark and asymmetric. Women average 236.8 minutes a day of unpaid work (housework, childcare and adult care) to men's 104.9 — a gap of 131.9 minutes, meaning women do 2.26 times as much. The largest single piece is routine housework: women 201.0 minutes versus men 90.0. Men compensate with paid work: 228.3 minutes a day to women's 128.8, a 99.4-minute lead. But the paid surplus does not fully cancel the unpaid one. Add the two together and women's total work day (365.6 minutes) is 32.5 minutes longer than men's (333.2) — the 'second shift' visible in the numbers, and consistent with OECD findings that women's unpaid work is roughly twice men's.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_01: The gender gap in unpaid vs paid work (headline) ---
print("=== ana_01 ===")
gp = {}
for s,lab in [(1,'Men'),(2,'Women')]:
    sub = df[df['sex']==s]
    gp[lab] = {
        'paid': wmean(sub['paidwork'], sub['propwt']),
        'unpaid': wmean(sub['unpaid'], sub['propwt']),
        'housework': wmean(sub['housework'], sub['propwt']),
        'childcare': wmean(sub['childcare'], sub['propwt']),
        'total': wmean(sub['totalwork'], sub['propwt']),
    }
for lab in ['Men','Women']:
    g=gp[lab]
    print(f"{lab}: paid={g['paid']:.1f} ({hm(g['paid'])}) unpaid={g['unpaid']:.1f} ({hm(g['unpaid'])}) "
          f"housework={g['housework']:.1f} childcare={g['childcare']:.1f} total={g['total']:.1f} ({hm(g['total'])})")
print(f"Unpaid gap (W-M): {gp['Women']['unpaid']-gp['Men']['unpaid']:.1f} min; ratio W/M = {gp['Women']['unpaid']/gp['Men']['unpaid']:.2f}")
print(f"Paid gap (M-W):   {gp['Men']['paid']-gp['Women']['paid']:.1f} min")
print(f"Total work gap (W-M): {gp['Women']['total']-gp['Men']['total']:.1f} min")
raw_evidence.output:
Men: paid=228.3 (3h48m) unpaid=104.9 (1h45m) housework=90.0 childcare=11.3 total=333.2 (5h33m)
Women: paid=128.8 (2h09m) unpaid=236.8 (3h57m) housework=201.0 childcare=30.2 total=365.6 (6h06m)
Unpaid gap (W-M): 131.9 min; ratio W/M = 2.26
Paid gap (M-W): 99.4 min
Total work gap (W-M): 32.5 min

raw_evidence.label: The time-use diary method and the 1,440-minute budget
raw_evidence.content: Time-use research rests on a simple but powerful constraint: a day has exactly 24 hours, or 1,440 minutes, and they cannot be created or destroyed — only reallocated. Unlike survey questions that ask people to estimate how much they 'usually' work or sleep (which produce notoriously inflated, socially desirable answers), the diary asks what someone was doing at each moment of a specific day. Because every activity competes for the same fixed budget, the diary captures trade-offs that stylised questions miss: more screen time must come out of something else. The MTUS harmonises diaries collected at 5-, 10-, 15-, or 30-minute intervals and on free-interval instruments into common categories, so a Korean diary from 2019 and a British diary from 1974 can be placed on the same axis.

raw_evidence.label: Why this data matters

Unpaid domestic and care work, largely invisible in GDP, has been valued at a substantial fraction of national output; the UNDP and others argue that ignoring it systematically undervalues women's contribution to the economy. raw_evidence.label: The established gender gap in unpaid work
raw_evidence.content: The single most robust finding in the time-use literature is that women perform far more unpaid domestic and care work than men, while men do more paid work — a division that persists even where women's paid employment has risen sharply. The gap varies enormously by place: under an hour a day in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, but over 200 minutes in countries such as Türkiye, Portugal and Mexico. raw_evidence.label: The unpaid-work gender gap: women do 2.3x men's
raw_evidence.content: Across all 1.4 million weighted diary days, the division of labour is stark and asymmetric. Women average 236.8 minutes a day of unpaid work (housework, childcare and adult care) to men's 104.9 — a gap of 131.9 minutes, meaning women do 2.26 times as much. The largest single piece is routine housework: women 201.0 minutes versus men 90.0. Men compensate with paid work: 228.3 minutes a day to women's 128.8, a 99.4-minute lead. But the paid surplus does not fully cancel the unpaid one. Add the two together and women's total work day (365.6 minutes) is 32.5 minutes longer than men's (333.2) — the 'second shift' visible in the numbers, and consistent with OECD findings that women's unpaid work is roughly twice men's.

Women average 236.8 minutes a day of unpaid work (housework, childcare and adult care) to men's 104.9 — a gap of 131.9 minutes, meaning women do 2.26 times as much. The largest single piece is routine housework: women 201.0 minutes versus men 90.0. Men compensate with paid work: 228.3 minutes a day to women's 128.8, a 99.4-minute lead. raw_evidence.label: Why this data matters
raw_evidence.content: Time is the one resource distributed perfectly equally — everyone gets exactly 24 hours — and yet how it is spent maps almost every social inequality we care about: who does the unpaid work that keeps households running, who has leisure, who sleeps enough, how technology rewires daily life. Unpaid domestic and care work, largely invisible in GDP, has been valued at a substantial fraction of national output; the UNDP and others argue that ignoring it systematically undervalues women's contribution to the economy. Time-use diaries are the instrument that makes this invisible labour countable. A blog grounded in the MTUS is therefore a blog about fairness, measured in minutes.

raw_evidence.label: The established gender gap in unpaid work
raw_evidence.content: The single most robust finding in the time-use literature is that women perform far more unpaid domestic and care work than men, while men do more paid work — a division that persists even where women's paid employment has risen sharply. OECD analysis across countries finds women average about four hours a day of unpaid household and care work, roughly twice men's, and across 23 European countries women spend about 262 minutes versus men's 141 — a gap of roughly two hours every day. The gap varies enormously by place: under an hour a day in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, but over 200 minutes in countries such as Türkiye, Portugal and Mexico. Routine housework is the single largest component of unpaid work for both sexes. This is the benchmark against which the MTUS housework and childcare numbers should be read.

raw_evidence.label: What the MTUS is and how it was built
raw_evidence.content: The Multinational Time Use Study (MTUS) is the world's longest-running cross-national archive of how ordinary people actually spend their day. Its method is the time-use diary: respondents record, episode by episode, what they were doing across a full 24-hour day, which is then harmonised into comparable activity totals measured in minutes per day (every diary day sums to 1,440 minutes). The Harmonized Aggregated File (HAF) used here collapses each diary into 25 standard activity categories — sleep, paid work, food preparation, cleaning and laundry, childcare, screen/computer time, leisure, travel, and so on — alongside demographics (country, survey year, sex, age, employment, education) and survey weights. Version 11 of the database, released in 2024 by the Centre for Time Use Research, contains 1,429,253 diary days drawn from 108 surveys across 25 countries, spanning 1961 to 2023. It is curated and harmonised rather than a single raw survey, which is exactly what makes cross-country and cross-decade comparison possible.

Because every activity competes for the same fixed budget, the diary captures trade-offs that stylised questions miss: more screen time must come out of something else. The MTUS harmonises diaries collected at 5-, 10-, 15-, or 30-minute intervals and on free-interval instruments into common categories, so a Korean diary from 2019 and a British diary from 1974 can be placed on the same axis.

raw_evidence.label: Survey weights and comparability caveats
raw_evidence.content: Raw diary counts are not representative populations. The MTUS provides two weights: OCOMBWT, the original survey weight supplied by each national statistics office, and PROPWT, a 'proposed weight' created by CTUR that additionally corrects for imbalances in which days of the week were sampled (weekends are under-collected in many surveys, yet a Sunday looks very different from a Tuesday). Low-quality diaries — flagged by the BADCASE variable — are given a weight of zero so they drop out of weighted estimates. All population means in this analysis are therefore PROPWT-weighted. The headline caveat for any cross-country comparison: countries were surveyed in different years, with different diary instruments and recall windows, so differences partly reflect when and how a country was measured, not only how its people live. These are harmonised but not identical instruments.

raw_evidence.label: The average human day, in minutes
raw_evidence.content: Pooled across every country and year and weighted to represent populations, the average diary day is dominated by three blocks. Sleep is by far the largest at 506.4 minutes (8h26m). Screen time — television, radio and computer combined — is the next single leisure block at 142.5 minutes (2h22m). raw_evidence.label: Who sleeps most and least (country ranking)
raw_evidence.content: Sleep varies by more than an hour and a half a day across countries. South Africa tops the ranking at 566.0 minutes (9h26m), followed by Armenia (554.8) and Bulgaria (554.5). At the bottom sit Austria (457.1, 7h37m), the United Kingdom (468.4) and South Korea (471.1, 7h51m) — the latter consistent with Korea's reputation as one of the most sleep-deprived, overworked societies. The 109-minute spread between South Africa and Austria is larger than most individual activity categories. Some of this gap reflects genuine differences in daily life; some reflects different survey years and diary conventions across countries, so the ranking should be read as indicative rather than a precise league table.

    print(f"{name:16s} {v:6.1f} ({hm(v)})  n={n}")

raw_evidence.label: Survey weights and comparability caveats
raw_evidence.content: Raw diary counts are not representative populations. The MTUS provides two weights: OCOMBWT, the original survey weight supplied by each national statistics office, and PROPWT, a 'proposed weight' created by CTUR that additionally corrects for imbalances in which days of the week were sampled (weekends are under-collected in many surveys, yet a Sunday looks very different from a Tuesday). Low-quality diaries — flagged by the BADCASE variable — are given a weight of zero so they drop out of weighted estimates. All population means in this analysis are therefore PROPWT-weighted. The headline caveat for any cross-country comparison: countries were surveyed in different years, with different diary instruments and recall windows, so differences partly reflect when and how a country was measured, not only how its people live. These are harmonised but not identical instruments.

South Korea, despite its overwork reputation, sits high at 210.7 minutes — but is below several Central and Eastern European countries, a reminder that population-wide diary averages mix employment rates, part-time prevalence and survey timing, not just the intensity of those who work. The Netherlands' low figure reflects its well-known high rate of part-time employment. These are population averages, not averages among workers.

South Korea has long been one of the most overworked societies in the developed world; its government has repeatedly legislated to cut a 68-hour legal work week, and Koreans are frequently reported among the shortest sleepers and longest workers in international comparisons. sentences.summary: det_04: The established gender gap in unpaid work. Source: OECD — Persistent gender gaps in paid and unpaid work (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/gender-equality-in-a-changing-world_e808086) Facts: Women average ~4 hours/day of unpaid work, about twice men's; Across 23 European countries women spend ~262 min vs men's 141 min on unpaid work | det_05: Gender convergence over cohorts. Source: Gender Symmetry, Gender Convergence and Historical Work-time Invariance (CTUR WP 2/2018) (https://www.timeuse.org/sites/default/files/2018-02/CTUR%20WP%202%202018_0.pdf) Facts: Regular but incomplete gender convergence: men do more unpaid work, women more paid work over cohorts; Total work time (paid + unpaid) shows historical near-invariance

raw_evidence.label: The established gender gap in unpaid work
raw_evidence.content: The single most robust finding in the time-use literature is that women perform far more unpaid domestic and care work than men, while men do more paid work — a division that persists even where women's paid employment has risen sharply. OECD analysis across countries finds women average about four hours a day of unpaid household and care work, roughly twice men's, and across 23 European countries women spend about 262 minutes versus men's 141 — a gap of roughly two hours every day. The gap varies enormously by place: under an hour a day in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, but over 200 minutes in countries such as Türkiye, Portugal and Mexico. Routine housework is the single largest component of unpaid work for both sexes. This is the benchmark against which the MTUS housework and childcare numbers should be read.

sources.title: OECD — Persistent gender gaps in paid and unpaid work
facts: Women average ~4 hours/day of unpaid work, about twice men's
Across 23 European countries women spend ~262 min vs men's 141 min on unpaid work
Gender unpaid-work gaps exceed 200 min/day in Türkiye, Portugal, Mexico and are under 60 min/day in Denmark, Norway, Sweden

raw_evidence.label: Gender convergence over cohorts
raw_evidence.content: Time-use scholars have documented a slow but strikingly regular convergence: across successive birth cohorts and survey waves, men have taken on more unpaid work and women more paid work, narrowing both gaps in nearly every country studied. The convergence is real but incomplete — it has slowed, and in some domains stalled, well before parity. Research using these very diaries describes a 'gender convergence' alongside a near-invariance in total work time (paid plus unpaid combined), implying that what changes is the mix of who does what, more than the total burden. This is the interpretive frame for any decade-over-decade trend the analyst finds.

sentences.summary: det_07: The rise of screen and ICT time. Source: MTUS Codebook — 25-category activity grouping (https://www.timeuse.org) Facts: TVRADIO = watch television, listen to radio; COMPINT = e-mail, web, program, computer games

raw_evidence.label: The rise of screen and ICT time
raw_evidence.content: One of the clearest secular trends in modern time-use data is the growth of screen-based and information-and-communication-technology (ICT) time. The MTUS captures this through two categories: TVRADIO (watching television and listening to radio), historically the dominant leisure activity of the late 20th century, and COMPINT (e-mail, web, programming, computer games), which barely existed before the late 1990s and has expanded rapidly since. Because diaries record a single primary activity per moment, these totals likely undercount true device exposure (people scroll while doing other things), but the harmonised categories still let us watch the centre of gravity of leisure shift from the broadcast screen toward the personal, networked screen across the decades the MTUS spans.

raw_evidence.label: The screen shifts from broadcast to computer
raw_evidence.content: The MTUS captures the digital transition in slow motion. raw_evidence.label: How the average day changed: more sleep and screens, less work
raw_evidence.content: Comparing diaries before 1980 with diaries from 2010 onward shows where the modern day diverged from the 20th-century one. Reported sleep rose sharply (+90.0 minutes), though much of this reflects changing diary conventions and the mix of countries measured early versus late, so it should be read cautiously. More robustly: TV and radio rose +45.9 minutes, computer and internet appeared from nothing (+17.0), paid work fell -22.8 minutes and housework fell -13.9. Childcare rose +6.3 and sport +5.8. The direction is consistent with the broad story of the era: less time at work and on housework, more on screens and (modestly) on active leisure and hands-on parenting.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_07: The average day, then vs now (1960s/70s vs 2010s/20s) ---
print("=== ana_07 ===")
early = df[df['year']<1980]; late = df[df['year']>=2010]
chg_cats=[('sleep','Sleep'),('paidwork','Paid work'),('housework','Housework'),
          ('tvradio','TV & radio'),('compint','Computer & internet'),('eatdrink','Eating'),
          ('commute','Commute'),('sportex','Sport & exercise'),('childcare','Childcare')]
print(f"early n={len(early)} (yr<1980); late n={len(late)} (yr>=2010)")
for col,lab in chg_cats:
    e=wmean(early[col],early['propwt']); l=wmean(late[col],late['propwt'])
    print(f"{lab:22s} {e:6.1f} -> {l:6.1f}  ({l-e:+.1f})")

raw_evidence.content: The MTUS captures the digital transition in slow motion. Computer and internet time (e-mail, web, programming, games) was effectively zero in the 1960s and 1970s, registered a trace 0.4 minutes/day in the 1980s, then climbed to 5.3 minutes in the 1990s, 14.1 in the 2000s, 16.6 in the 2010s and 19.5 in the 2020s. raw_evidence.label: Gender convergence over cohorts
raw_evidence.content: Time-use scholars have documented a slow but strikingly regular convergence: across successive birth cohorts and survey waves, men have taken on more unpaid work and women more paid work, narrowing both gaps in nearly every country studied. The convergence is real but incomplete — it has slowed, and in some domains stalled, well before parity. Research using these very diaries describes a 'gender convergence' alongside a near-invariance in total work time (paid plus unpaid combined), implying that what changes is the mix of who does what, more than the total burden. This is the interpretive frame for any decade-over-decade trend the analyst finds.

raw_evidence.label: Women work more total hours — the 'second shift'
raw_evidence.content: When paid and unpaid work are added together, multiple cross-national analyses conclude that women work slightly more total hours than men in most countries — the long hours of unpaid domestic and care work more than offset men's longer paid hours. The World Economic Forum, summarising OECD data, reported that women work on average nearly an hour longer per day than men once unpaid work is counted. This is the empirical backbone of the 'second shift' idea: paid-work parity on paper can coexist with a heavier overall workload at home.

raw_evidence.label: The unpaid-work gap narrows as men step up
raw_evidence.content: Watching the unpaid-work gender gap across decades shows the convergence the literature predicts — driven mostly by men. Setting aside the sparse, convention-affected 1960s, the gap ran 129.6 minutes in the 1970s, widened to 156.5 in the 1980s, then narrowed steadily: 143.7 (1990s), 135.6 (2000s), 89.4 (2010s) and 88.6 (2020s). The mechanism is asymmetric: women's unpaid minutes drifted down only modestly (260.8 in the 1980s to 222.7 in the 2020s) while men's rose substantially (104.3 to 134.0). In other words, the gap closed less because women did dramatically less and more because men finally did more — but the gap is still roughly an hour and a half a day, far from parity.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: Gender convergence in unpaid work across decades ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
rows=[]
for dec,sub in df.groupby('decade'):
    if pd.isna(dec) or len(sub)<500: continue
    m=sub[sub['sex']==1]; w=sub[sub['sex']==2]
    wm=wmean(w['unpaid'],w['propwt']); mm=wmean(m['unpaid'],m['propwt'])
    rows.append((int(dec), wm, mm, wm-mm, len(sub)))
rows=sorted(rows)
for dec,wmv,mmv,gap,n in rows:
    print(f"{dec}s  W={wmv:6.1f}  M={mmv:6.1f}  gap={gap:6.1f}  n={n}")

sentences.context: Time is the most evenly distributed resource on earth and one of the most unevenly spent.
sentences.summary: det_09: Why this data matters. Source: UNDP — Valuing women's unrecognized contribution to the economy (https://www.undp.org/latin-america/blog/missing-piece-valuing-womens-unrecognize) Facts: Unpaid care and domestic work is largely excluded from GDP and disproportionately performed by women

raw_evidence.label: Why this data matters
raw_evidence.content: Time is the one resource distributed perfectly equally — everyone gets exactly 24 hours — and yet how it is spent maps almost every social inequality we care about: who does the unpaid work that keeps households running, who has leisure, who sleeps enough, how technology rewires daily life. Unpaid domestic and care work, largely invisible in GDP, has been valued at a substantial fraction of national output; the UNDP and others argue that ignoring it systematically undervalues women's contribution to the economy. Time-use diaries are the instrument that makes this invisible labour countable. A blog grounded in the MTUS is therefore a blog about fairness, measured in minutes.

raw_evidence.label: The unpaid-work gender gap: women do 2.3x men's
raw_evidence.content: Across all 1.4 million weighted diary days, the division of labour is stark and asymmetric. Women average 236.8 minutes a day of unpaid work (housework, childcare and adult care) to men's 104.9 — a gap of 131.9 minutes, meaning women do 2.26 times as much. The largest single piece is routine housework: women 201.0 minutes versus men 90.0. Men compensate with paid work: 228.3 minutes a day to women's 128.8, a 99.4-minute lead. But the paid surplus does not fully cancel the unpaid one. Add the two together and women's total work day (365.6 minutes) is 32.5 minutes longer than men's (333.2) — the 'second shift' visible in the numbers, and consistent with OECD findings that women's unpaid work is roughly twice men's.

        'childcare': wmean(sub['childcare'], sub['propwt']),
        'total': wmean(sub['totalwork'], sub['propwt']),
    }
for lab in ['Men','Women']:

          f"housework={g['housework']:.1f} childcare={g['childcare']:.1f} total={g['total']:.1f} ({hm(g['total'])})")
